## What is R?

When you collect fisheries data, you need a way to make sense of it: to add up catches,
compare landing sites, or spot a month when something looks wrong. **R is a free tool made
for exactly this.**

Think of R as a careful, very fast assistant. You give it a short written instruction, such as
*"add up the weight"* or *"show me only the landings from Vanga"*. It does the work exactly, and straight
away. Ten records or one hundred thousand, it makes no difference. It is the same tool used by the
scientists who prepare your data.

A spreadsheet like Excel is fine for a small table. R goes further in three ways. It does not slow down
with large amounts of data. It does not make copy-and-paste mistakes. And it remembers every step, so the
same work can be repeated next month without starting over.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What is this page, then?

This page runs R **right inside your web browser**. There is nothing to download or install —
it just works, and it is free.

You do **not** need to be a programmer. In these lessons you will mostly **press a button** and
change a few small things. And **you cannot break anything**: if something looks wrong, just
press **Run** again.
:::

## How it works: press Run

Below is a small table of fish landings — just six rows, so it is easy to read.

The first box runs **on its own** when the page opens. Look for the green **▶ Run** button on the box:
you can press it to run the box again.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The first time, R has to wake up

When you open a lesson, your browser quietly downloads R. **This can take a minute on a slow
connection** — and only the first time.

While it is waiting you will see a small **spinning circle** on the box, and pressing **Run** will seem
to do nothing. That is not a fault. Wait for the spinner to stop, and the answer will appear.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# Switch on dplyr, the toolkit these lessons use.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

# A small example table: six catches from two areas.
landings_example <- data.frame(
  landing_date = c("2024-01-05", "2024-01-05", "2024-01-06", "2024-01-06", "2024-01-07", "2024-01-07"),
  gaul_2_name  = c("Shimoni", "Shimoni", "Vanga", "Shimoni", "Vanga", "Vanga"),
  catch_taxon  = c("Tilapia", "Snapper", "Tilapia", "Octopus", "Snapper", "Tilapia"),
  catch_kg     = c(12, 5, 8, 3, 6, 10)
)

landings_example
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** a table with **6 rows** and **4 columns**.

The headings look odd, so let's name them now. They are the **real headings from your own data**, and
you will meet them again in every lesson:

- `landing_date` — the day the catch came to shore
- `gaul_2_name` — the **district**, or area
- `catch_taxon` — the **kind of fish**
- `catch_kg` — the **weight**, in kilograms
:::

## Now you try: press Run yourself

This box adds up all the weights. **Press the ▶ Run button** to see the answer.

The `$` sign just means "this column of that table". So `landings_example$catch_kg` is the `catch_kg`
column of the `landings_example` table, and `sum()` adds it up.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
sum(landings_example$catch_kg)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** `44`. That is the total weight of all six catches, in kilograms.
:::

## Change one thing, then run again

You do **not** need to understand the instruction below yet. That comes in the next lessons. For now, just
see how easy it is to change an answer.

The word `filter` means "keep only the rows I ask for". This box keeps only the catches **heavier than
5 kg**. **Change the `5` to `9`**, then press **Run** again.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
filter(landings_example, catch_kg > 5)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Try it:** with `5` you see **four** rows. Change it to `9` and press Run. Now you see only the **two**
catches above 9 kg.

That is all "coding" is here. Small instructions you can change, with the answer right away.
:::

## This works on YOUR data too

The table above was made up. In the next lessons the table will be **your real landing records**. It is
the same data you can open in **Data Download**, from your own district.

Here is a peek. Press **Run** to load the first rows of your data:

{{< include _landings-data.qmd >}}

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| input:
#|   - landings_data
# quarto-live converts the JS array of row objects into an R data.frame automatically.
landings <- tryCatch(as.data.frame(landings_data), error = function(e) data.frame())

if (nrow(landings) == 0) {
  cat("Your data will appear here once you are signed in to the platform.\n")
} else {
  cat("Loaded", nrow(landings), "of your landing records.\n")
  head(landings)
}
```

## What you will learn next

Each lesson is short and uses your own data. You will learn to answer everyday questions:

- 🔎 **Find the rows you need** — *"Show me only the landings from Vanga."* — *"Only last month."*
- 📋 **Pick the columns you need** — *"I only want the date, the district and the weight."*
- ➕ **Add it up** — *"What is the total catch at each district?"* — *"Which gear catches the most?"*

You will only ever **press Run** and **change small things**. Take the lessons in order.
